source_refs.note: Types of Inhibitors: a main subheading of 5.6 Enzyme inhibition, its own page (owner 2026-11-04); PDF 137-138.

blocks.text: Two general classes of inhibitors are recognized; competitive and non-competitive inhibitors. A competitive inhibitor resembles the enzyme’s substrate. It competes with substrate for the same binding site on enzyme. When competitive inhibitor is selected by binding site, it blocks active site and does not permit substrate from attaching. Thus, it prevents enzyme from acting (Figure 5.9).

Competitive inhibitors are used as antibiotics to kill bacteria. These inhibitor molecules are similar in structure to bacterial enzymes which are necessary for their life. The inhibitors bind and inhibit the enzymes of bacteria.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: A competitive inhibitor resembles the substrate, not the enzyme (as the text above says). These antibiotic molecules are similar in structure to the substrates of bacterial enzymes which are necessary for the life of bacteria; so they bind to and block the active sites of those enzymes.

blocks.alt: Two stages. A kidney-shaped enzyme with a V-shaped active site; a substrate and an inhibitor of similar fitting shape both head for it (Competition between substrate and inhibitor). Then the inhibitor sits in the active site and the substrate is left outside (Inhibitor attaches with active site and blocks it); a dotted arrow leads to No products. Labels: Substrate, Inhibitor, Active site, Enzyme.
blocks.caption: Figure 5.9: Competitive inhibition of an enzyme (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 5.9).

blocks.text: The enzyme succinic dehydrogenase catalyses the oxidation of succinic acid to fumaric acid. Malonic acid has structural similarity with substrate (succinic acid). So, both of them compete for active site of enzyme. Malonic acid is selected by active site and thus blocks it.

A non-competitive inhibitor has no real structural similarity to substrate. So, it does not enter active site. Instead, it binds enzyme at other places. Its binding alters the shape of enzyme so that active site does not fit substrate and so enzyme is inhibited (Figure 5.10).

blocks.alt: Three stages joined by arrows. A round enzyme with a wedge-shaped active site that fits a cone-shaped substrate, and a second small pocket at its lower left; a yellow inhibitor lies nearby. The inhibitor binds the side pocket (Enzyme-inhibitor complex). The active site then changes to a narrow straight slot that no longer fits the substrate (Shape of active site altered); a dotted arrow leads to No products. Labels: Substrate, Active site, Enzyme, Inhibitor.
blocks.caption: Figure 5.10: Non-competitive inhibition of an enzyme (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 5.10).

blocks.text: For example; two substrates i.e., succinic acid and CoA react to form succinyl-CoA. This reaction is catalysed by enzyme succinyl-CoA synthetase. After its formation, the product i.e., succinyl CoA acts as a non-competitive inhibitor and binds with enzyme. Thus, enzyme is inhibited and no more succinyl-CoA is produced.
The action of any inhibitor can be irreversible or reversible, depending upon the kind of bond formed between inhibitor and enzyme.

Irreversible inhibitors make covalent bonds with enzyme. Such inhibitors cannot be released by dilution or dialysis or by increasing the concentration of substrate. for example, penicillin permanently disables the enzyme responsible for building bacterial cell walls.

Reversible inhibitors make weak bonds (e.g., hydrogen bonds) with enzyme. Such inhibitors can be released and the inhibition caused by them can be neutralized by increasing the concentration of substrate. for example, malonate is a reversible inhibitor. It temporarily slows down the reaction by blocking the enzyme succinate dehydrogenase, which is involved in cellular respiration. This inhibition can be reversed when malonate is removed.
